Interactive timeline

The printing press
& worldwide change.

How did producing a book or pamphlet change from being a highly specialized task performed by scribes to a massive industrial process that allowed information to become widely available?

8 of 8 timeline entries shown

  1. Before c. 1450 / books before prinitng press

    Books written by the hands of scribes

    In medieval Europe to make a copy of a book, scribes had to do the entire process by hand, this involved copying the text by hand, binding the pages and assembling the book. Professional scribes of this era used quills to write and the process required intense focus, as mistakes could remain on the print and each copy of a book required repeating this process all over again.

    How did this impact the world?

    Why was it so labor intensive?: Instead of paper, parchment was the main thing used to write books which had to be prepared from animal skins. This required a whole process of preparing the parchment that took extra time. In order to write or copy books, scribes spent long hours everyday writing every word by hand using a quill, the entire thing took months or even years depending on the length of the book being copied. Scribes also suffered pain from bad posture constant writing, add on top of that the worry of making a mistake, which if too severe could be very difficult to correct and would likely stay on the copy.

    How did this limit access?: The need for this kind of process before the invention of the Gutenberg press meant that only very wealthy people could afford to purchase books or bibles. The fact that every copy made took months or years made it incredibly expensive for peasants or average people of this time to own books. This financial and labor aspect of it severely limited who could access information and in fact most christians of the time could not afford to own a copy of the bible.

    Historical background: This section serves to clarify that while this was the main way of copying books in Europe during this time, some Asian societies had already started to develop forms of printing by using wooden or clay tablets which could be dipped in ink and stamped onto parchment or early forms of paper to copy text. This however was not highly efficient when it came to copying entire books and thus was not popularized worldwide.

    Information sources
    • Cambridge: preparation, copying, and physical labor
    • British Library: scribal tools and training
  2. c. 1440–1455 / Invention of the gutenberg press

    Gutenberg makes the copying of books easier

    Johannes Gutenberg, who was a German inventor born in 1400 developed a system combining movable metal type with a mechanical press in Mainz, Germany. The Gutenberg press had been in development since the 1440s and was used to begin printing the bible in the yar 1450. By 1450, the press was fully functional and the printing of the Gutenberg bible began. By 1455 about 180 copies of this bible had been printed, some on parchment and most copies on paper.

    How did this impact the world?

    What changed in production?: Instead of scribes handwriting every copy of a book, in this case the most noteworthy being the bible, the use of this new technology developed by Gutenberg allowed workers to arrange the letters for a specific page, dip in ink and press onto paper to print it as many times as they wanted, this could be done a 100 times for each page, for example and by the end all that was left was to assemble the pages in the correct order, and 100 copies of the book were ready. This drastically reduced the time need to copy books and therefore they became more accessible, although still quite expensive.

    Not an Instant replacement: While the technology for the exact replication of books had been developed, the change was not yet a massive revolution until some years later when massive publishers started to grow and needed the means by which to mass print.

    Information sources
    • Library of Congress: Gutenberg’s Bible and earlier Korean metal type
    • American Printing History Association: typecasting and hand-press printing
  3. 1469 / Massive printing centers

    Venice becomes the center of book publishing in Europe

    Printing reached Venice in 1469, over a decade after the Gutenberg Bible had been successfully printed hundreds of times. The city became the largest publishing place for books in Europe as a result of demand for books and economic growth of this city at the time. As the market for printed books grew publishers developed their own engravings on them to distinguish themselves among others. The city's trade with the rest of the world also made books more accessible to places which at this point in time lacked the technology or means by which to develop prints and make books avaliable to their population.

    How did this impact the world?

    How did this impact the world?: The rise of publishing met the demands of a growing market for books and prints of texts which fueled the need for more presses and really took off with the new technology becoming widely adopted rather than being a single machine in Germany. This was the turning point where mass printing became the norm and manuscripts were no longer as needed.

    Information sources
    • Morgan Library & Museum: Venice, publishing, and artists
  4. By 1501 / Expansion of the technology

    Printed books become widespread

    Estimates show that around 250 European printing centers had been established around Europe by 1501, with estimates putting the quanity of written works at around 27,000 titles, and a circulation of roughly 10 million books. This massive change in literary accessibility in Europe just a few decades after Gutenberg's invention proved that the way which society could get their hands on information had completely changed. Now more than ever, the average person might be able to own a book, where less than a century prior this was virtually impossible. The process by which people could read not only impacted the economy but also the education of society improved as more people could partake in reading literary work which were at a time exclusive to the wealthiest people.

    How did this impact the world?

    Why did readers want printed books?: Readers during this period were primarily interested in books that were about natural sciences, religion and law. The printing of books made reproduction faster and cheaper, which benefited both publishers and the growing interest in reading. Publishing in multiple languages also broadened the amount of people who could read these printed books and grew the market further leading to higher demand.

    How did shift the culture?: More copies being printed meant that more people had access to literary and scientific works than ever before, this rise in information fueled the renaissance era and lead to massive cultural shifts about the ways that people viewed the world with many adhering to "Humanist" values that saw benefit in reading classic literature and being virtuous.

    The impact on Labor: Although massive improvements had occured in the realm of access to books and information, the labor required to make copies had not changed much since the invention of the printing press by Gutenberg and the process by which these prints were manufactured had not reached it potential.

    Information sources
    • Getty: estimates, readership, subjects, and book production
  5. 1517–1521 / Religion & authority

    Printing fuels the Protestant Reformation

    Martin Luther’s criticism of indulgences in 1517 and his publishing of the 95 Theses which heavily criticized the Roman Catholic Church changed from being mostly contained within private meeting and small audiences to being widespread and printed all over the place, which allowed even the poorest people to read it and add to the cultural shift and questioning of the church.

    How did this impact the world?

    How did this change religious authority?: Luther’s writings challenged the Catholic Church’s practices and authority. Printing gave people the ability to spread their ideas among large groups of people and this eventually spread the sentiment as people started to organize and push for change; this would not have been possible if it were not for the ability to print papers and distribute them among thousands of people.

    Reading and language: Publishers appealed to new readers with simplified religious texts derived from latin into german translations which were more affordable than full texts and promoted discourse among people within those societies about theology and their own beliefs as well as the institution of the Roman Catholic Church.

    Spread due to Conflict: The more that pamphlets were distributed, the more people identified themselves with the cause of Martin Luther, which made them even more interested in reading his works. In 1520, Luther was excommunitcated by Pope Leo X who also demanded that his books be burned. Burnings took place in several European cities, however this did not silence the cause and instead made people want to read about it and why the books were being burned, it turned into a battle against censorship and the spread of ideas supported by the ability to print more pamphlets.

    Information sources
    • Cambridge University Press: print and the Reformation
    • Lutheran School of Theology at Chicago: book burning and excommunication
  6. 1543 and the 1600s / Science & The sharing of knowledge

    Printed scientific works expanded knowledge and discovery

    Copernicus, a polish polymath and astronomer born in 1743 published De revolutionibus in 1543, this text was the first that explained a system by which the Earth moves around the Sun. While contradictory to previous understandings, its print and replication allowed for people to read it and make their own observations about it, whether they agreed or disagreed, the ability to share knowledge within the scientific community allowed people who lived far away to be able to come up with rebuttals and even extensions of the theories developed by others, and publish these for the general audience to read and analyze.

    How did this impact the world?

    This supported the Scientific Revolution: Printing enabled standardized texts and images to reach multiple readers and it not only allowed for the sharing of ideas, but also of complex diagrams and illustrations of such ideas. These were important to develop the scientific understanding of the time period and was an impulse for the scientific revolution and the development over time of more complex systems by which we can understand the world around like; for example: mathematics, astronomy and biology and something as basic as the scientific method which became standardized and is now accepted by the scientific community as the way to conduct experiments and share knowledge.

    A foundation for further knowledge: Although the claims in these early scientific journals were not accurate, at least not entirely, the ability of a scientist to take anothers work and expand on it using their own experiments and observations set the stage for modern day peer reviews and the debating of new theories. This mainly lead to the mass cooperation of people to develop new understandings of the world through collaboration.

    Information sources
    • Library of Congress: Copernicus’s 1543 publication
    • Oxford History of Science Museum: scientific images and standardized information
  7. 1814 and the 1800s / Industrial production & newspapers

    Steam-powered presses increase the scale of news access

    Friedrich Koenig, an inventor born in Eisleben, Germany in 1774 invented a steam-powered cylinder press in 1810. This revolutionary machine printed "The Times" newspaper issue of November 29, 1814 in London. It was able to print around 1,100 sheets per hour. This replaced human labor with a rolling cylinder and mechanical energy powered by steam and massively cut down on the amount of time required to print. This revolutionized printing forever and made news more accessible than at any time in history.

    How did this impact the world?

    How did it change production?: Newspaper demand called for faster machines, Koenig's invention set the framework for the development of later nineteenth-century printing presses that used more cylinders, and rolls of paper which saw a significant increase in efficiency and speed compared to the inital two cylinder press by Koenig. The development of mechanical folding of pages over time also added to the speed at which newspapers could be developed.

    From individual devices to an industrial system: The change was seen with small adjustments over time and eventually the single machine evolved into the use of large scale industrial centers for printing works at rapid scales with dozens of these steam powered presses. By the late 1800s, newspapers had become easy to acquire and the news spread very quickly which resulted in a more informed society and influenced how news would be spread over the next century.

    Information sources
    • Library of Congress: 1814 press, cylinder printing, paper rolls, and folding
  8. 2026 / The Internet and e-books

    Printing is no longer needed to access information

    The rise of the internet and digitalization of the world allows readers to access a wide array of books and texts of any sort in 2026 for free. Project Gutenberg, for example, contains a library of thousands of free eBooks on its website which range from scientific works to classic literature. This means that unlike in the past, people all over the world can download books for free without the need to wait for prints to be made and shipped long distances. The ability to use formats like PDF to download books makes distributing copies instantaneous.

    How did this impact the world?

    How did the internet change access?: The internet did not only revolutionize access to information but also the way which people share information. Nowadays just a google search can provide near instant access to any question a person may have, which only a few decades away would require a trip to the library.

    From the printing press to present-day technology: The earlier timeline of this infographic shows how print helped scientific ideas and illustrations circulate. Modern research and engineering produced computers, cellphones and wifi, which created new faster and easier ways to share information. It illustrates the larger picture of how society has innovated and developed new ways to share information over centuries and how it only becomes easier. It can be said that a person today with a modern smartphone has more access to knowledge than any person or scholar in history.

    What changed?: Books can now circulate without paper or the need for taking up space on shelves, and information can be spread faster than ever. Although this requires a compatible device which can store the files containing the books or movies for instance, it is an option that did not exist in the past and has only benefited society as a whole by providing more information and access to knowledge in various formats at an affordable price or even for free as is the case for people who get books from online libraries which host free downloads.

    Information sources
    • Project Gutenberg: digital collection and free eBooks
    • CLIR, Frank Romano: E-Books and the Challenge of Preservation
